chapters.title: Chapter 2: Core RL Concepts a Trader Needs

lessons.title: Markov Decision Processes: The Mathematical Backbone of RL

body.text: Every RL algorithm in this course is, underneath, trying to solve the same mathematical object: a Markov Decision Process. Learn its five pieces properly here, and every later lesson, value functions, Q-learning, reward shaping, becomes a variation on a structure you already understand.

children.text: The Five Pieces of a Markov Decision Process

Chapter 1 described state, action, and reward informally, mapped onto a trader's own vocabulary. A Markov Decision Process, MDP, makes that formal by defining exactly five components. Everything this chapter and the next build, value functions, Q-learning, policy gradients, is machinery for solving this one structure.

body.caption: The Five Components of an MDP, in Trading Terms
headers: What It Means for a Trading Agent

cells: Every possible combination of market and position features the agent could observe: return, RSI, volatility, inventory, and so on
Every action the agent may take: discrete choices like buy, sell, hold, or a continuous position size
The probability of landing in state s' given the agent was in state s and took action a. In trading, shaped by every other market participant, not just the agent
The numerical feedback for that transition, built from P&L, transaction costs, and whatever risk penalty the designer chooses
A number between 0 and 1 controlling how much the agent values future reward relative to immediate reward

children.text: The Markov Property: Why the Present Is Supposed to Be Enough

body.latex: P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, \ldots, s_0, a_0) = P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)
body.caption: The Markov property: given the current state and action, the next state's probability does not depend on any earlier history. Everything relevant to the future is assumed to already be captured in the present state.

body.text: Raw price history is not Markovian. Tomorrow's return genuinely depends on more than today's closing price alone, momentum, volatility clustering, and regime all carry information from further back than one step. This is precisely why Chapter 1 spent so much effort on state design: features like a 5-day return or a rolling volatility measure exist to compress relevant history into the current state, so that state approximates the Markov property closely enough for the framework to work. An MDP with a poorly designed state is not really Markovian in practice, no matter what the math assumes.

children.text: Return and the Discount Factor: How Much Does the Future Matter

body.caption: The return: the total discounted reward an agent accumulates from time t onward. γ close to 1 means future rewards count almost as much as immediate ones; γ close to 0 makes the agent myopic, caring mostly about the very next reward.

children.text: The discount factor has to be chosen relative to how long an episode actually runs, and NSE's regular trading session gives a concrete way to see why.

body.label: NSE Regular Trading Session
body.context: 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM. A natural, ready-made step count for a one-day intraday MDP episode with one step per minute.

body.caption: How Much a Late-Session Reward Survives Discounting, by γ
headers: Steps Ahead (k, minutes into the session)

children.text: With γ = 0.99 and one step per minute, a reward earned at the closing bell is worth roughly 2% of one earned in the opening minute, for the agent's purposes it barely exists by the time training reinforces it. Push γ to 0.999 and that same closing-bell reward retains about 69% of its weight. For any strategy where what happens near the close genuinely matters, an end-of-day square-off under MIS margin rules, for instance, choosing γ too aggressively low is a silent way to train an agent that has effectively stopped caring about its own trading day before it ends.
Putting the Nifty 50 Futures Example Into Full MDP Notation

Chapter 1 built an informal state, action, reward picture for a Nifty 50 futures agent. In full MDP notation: S is every possible combination of the six features in that state vector, momentum, RSI, volume, India VIX, position, and unrealized P&L. A is the discrete set {buy, sell, hold}, or a continuous position size, depending on the design chosen. R(s,a,s') is the change in mark-to-market P&L, net of transaction costs, between one step and the next. The one piece deliberately left vague so far is P(s'|s,a), the transition function, because in trading it is not a clean, known table the way it might be in a board game. It is the combined effect of every other market participant's decisions, order flow, and news, none of which the agent controls or fully observes. This gap, a well-defined state, action, and reward but no usable model of P, is exactly what forces the choice this chapter's third lesson covers: model-free methods that never try to estimate P directly, learning a policy purely from experienced transitions instead.

body.code:
state = env.reset()
done = False
while not done:
    action = agent.select_action(state)
    next_state, reward, done, info = env.step(action)
    agent.learn(state, action, reward, next_state)
    state = next_state
body.caption: The MDP loop in code form. The agent never touches P(s'|s,a) directly, it only ever sees the (state, action, reward, next_state) tuple env.step() returns, which is exactly what a model-free method needs and all it gets.

body.title: Is This State Markovian Enough?
body.scenario: A researcher builds a state vector for an intraday Nifty 50 agent using only the current bid-ask spread and the current traded price, nothing else, arguing that these two numbers fully describe the state of the market right now.
body.prompt: Does this state satisfy the Markov property well enough for the MDP framework to work reliably? What is missing?
body.modelAnswer: No. Current spread and price alone discard information that genuinely affects what happens next: recent momentum (is the market trending or reverting), recent volatility (how large are typical moves right now), and the agent's own position (which affects whether a given price move helps or hurts, and how urgently the agent might need to act). Two moments with an identical spread and price can have very different likely next moves if one follows a sharp rally and the other follows a flat, quiet session, information the proposed state throws away entirely. A more Markovian state would add short-window return and volatility features, and the agent's own inventory, so that more of what actually predicts the next state is captured in the present observation rather than left to history the agent no longer has access to.

body.title: Reading the Discount Factor
body.question: An intraday agent's episode runs for the full 375-minute NSE trading session, one step per minute. Using a discount factor of γ = 0.99, roughly what does a reward earned at the very last minute of the session end up weighted at, relative to a reward earned in the first minute?
options: Almost the same weight, since 0.99 is close to 1
Roughly 2 percent of the first minute's weight, since 0.99 raised to 375 is a very small number
Exactly zero, since discounting eliminates all late rewards
The discount factor has no effect on how rewards late in an episode are weighted
body.explanation: 0.99 raised to the power 375 is approximately 0.02, meaning a reward earned in the session's final minute is discounted to roughly 2 percent of the weight given to a reward earned in the first minute. For an episode this long, γ = 0.99 makes the agent extremely myopic relative to the full session; a value like γ = 0.999 (0.999^375 ≈ 0.69) keeps late-session rewards meaningfully weighted, which matters for any strategy whose payoff, like an end-of-day square-off, depends on what happens near the close.

points: A Markov Decision Process is defined by five pieces: state space S, action space A, transition function P(s'|s,a), reward function R, and discount factor γ

The Markov property assumes the current state captures everything relevant to the future; raw market data does not satisfy this on its own, which is why deliberate state design from Chapter 1 matters so much

The discount factor γ controls how much future reward matters relative to immediate reward, and must be chosen relative to episode length; for a 375-minute NSE trading day, γ = 0.99 makes late-session rewards nearly worthless, while γ = 0.999 keeps them meaningfully weighted
The transition function P(s'|s,a) is rarely known or estimable in trading, since it reflects every other market participant's combined behavior, not something the agent controls
Not knowing P is exactly what pushes trading applications toward model-free RL methods, covered next, which learn a policy directly from experienced state, action, reward, next-state transitions
